newsitem.title: CANADA: CS Resources sees higher earnings in 1997.
newsitem.headline: CS Resources sees higher earnings in 1997.

text.p: CS Resources Ltd expects higher cash flow and earnings this year as it ramps up production from its primary and thermal heavy oil projects in Alberta and Saskatchewan, company president Dee Parkinson said on Tuesday.

Calgary-based CS, known for its high-tech drilling and production operations, was on track to post earnings of C$12.5 million and cash flow of C$60 million in 1997, Parkinson said at the company's annual meeting.
The company had earnings of C$10.3 million and cash flow of C$47.2 million last year.
Parkinson said production was projected to average 19,500 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 1997, up from 14,800.
She said operational setbacks at the company's Senlac thermal heavy oil project in Saskatchewan -- its first major steam injection operation -- moved production plans back by about one year.

Senlac, site of a twin-well steam assisted gravity drainage operation where one well injects steam into a wellbore and the other produces the bitumen, was set to pump an average of 2,000 barrels per day this year, down from its peak capacity of 5,000.
The problems occurred when sand screens, which allow bitumen to flow into the well while holding back sand particles, failed.
However, the company was within a few days of installing improved screens in the three well pairs and over the next several days would know if its efforts were successful, Parkinson said.
CS also planned to drill another well pair on the project, which is seen as a prototype to a much larger operation at Christina Lake in northern Alberta's Athabasca oil sands region.
Parkinson said Christina Lake had the potential to yield 50,000 barrels a day using thermal technology after startup around 2000.
Senlac was expected to reach its startup capacity in 1998, she said, adding that the project was giving CS return on its investment even at the lower output rate.

Meanwhile, CS chairman Dennis Sharp -- who founded the company in 1988 after gaining an exclusive license with France's Institut Francais du Petrole to use its horizontal drilling technology in Canada -- told shareholders Parkinson would assume the post of chief executive in August.

Sharp will then turn his attention to the newly founded CS International, which is examining projects to employ IFP technology at other heavy oil locations around the world in partnership with Chinese Petroleum Corp of Taiwan.

Sharp, who will remain as CS Resources' executive chairman, said the international arm was being structured to provide new cash flow to the Canadian company while not being a financial liability to it.
He said a project could be announced before the end of this year. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
